teaser: Why these articles sound like their author: a corpus, the voice memos, seven wording rules and a reader who corrects, with Claude explaining it from its side.
core_idea: The voice is not a setting but four inputs: a corpus of 86 articles, 51 from voice memos, each citing the ones before it; the memos themselves, which carry how the author thinks, the rhythm, the tangents and the order the points came in; seven wording rules learned one correction at a time and kept in the session's behaviour policy; and the author reading everything; the corrections have shifted from language to content, which is what a rules file does; and in a marked section Claude explains that it is continuing a body of work with the author's latest thinking in the author's own words rather than imitating a style, that the memo tells it how the author got there and not only what to write, and that nothing is trained, so the method transfers and the voice does not.

nodes.label: How do you make your AI sound so human?
nodes.summary: Asked by the person the walkthrough was written for; the better question is how to make it sound like one person.

nodes.label: The corpus
nodes.summary: 86 articles, about 347,000 words, 51 from memos, each citing the ones before it and resting on years of earlier writing; the vocabulary and the shape.

nodes.label: The memo
nodes.summary: Spoken, not typed: the rhythm, the tangents, five topics in one breath, the author's own phrases kept; how the author got there, not only what to write.

nodes.label: Seven wording rules
nodes.summary: No em-dashes, no unsupported absolutes, great not perfect, a ladder word banned, British English, plainer words, not prose; each a correction once, now a policy line restored after every summary.

nodes.label: The author reads everything
nodes.summary: A wrong word becomes a rule; a wrong point becomes a new version; the model never decides whether it sounds right.

nodes.label: Corrections moved from language to content
nodes.summary: In this session, 98 messages and 5 transcripts; one wording correction in two days, the rest content, direction and facts; a rules file makes a language correction once.

nodes.label: Not imitation but continuation
nodes.summary: Claude: with the linked articles open, the memo in the author's words and the banned words named, it continues a body of work rather than copying a style sample.

nodes.label: The method transfers, the voice does not
nodes.summary: Nothing is trained; one session's context; another author would need their corpus, memos, rules and reading, and most of those weeks are theirs.

nodes.label: Written in two voices
nodes.summary: The first half in the author's voice as every article is; the second marked as Claude speaking, the only place on the site it does.

quotes.text: The voice is not a setting.
A typed brief tells me what to write. A memo tells me how he got there.
quotes.why: Claude's reason the memo hypothesis holds.

quotes.text: The method is reusable; the voice is not.
